<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Frederica S. Wilson, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark Takano, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Jahana Hayes, Rep. Summer L. Lee, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 7661, the Stop the Sexualization of Children Act, would prohibit public schools, from using funds authorized under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965\1\ (ESEA) to ``develop, implement, facilitate, host, or promote'' programs, activities, literature, or materials for minors that include ``sexually oriented material.''\2\ This bill defines ``sexually oriented material'' as content depicting, describing, or simulating sexually explicit conduct,\3\ including material that exposes ``children to nude adults, individuals who are stripping, or lewd or lascivious dancing,'' and any material involving gender dysphoria or transgenderism.\4\ This bill is yet another attempt to promote culture wars by forcing public schools to follow partisan ideology in order to receive federal education funds. The bill negatively targets transgender people under the guise of stopping students from seeing sexually explicit material. In actuality, this bill does nothing to protect students in the classroom. However, it does have the potential to cause further marginalization and harm to trans students and potentially limit access to books, historical artifacts, and even state flags. Ultimately, this bill does nothing to address the actual challenges public K-12 schools are currently facing.
\1\20 U.S.C. Sec. 6301 et seq.
\2\Stop the Sexualization of Children Act, H.R. 7661 Sec. 2, 119th Cong. (2026).
\3\The bill incorporates by reference parts of the definition of ``sexually explicit conduct'' from 18 U.S.C. Sec. 2256(2)(A)-(B). Id.
\4\H.R. 7661 Sec. 2, 119th Cong. (2026).
SUMMARY OF CONCERNS
This Bill Aims To Infuse Curriculum and All Other Aspects of Public
Schools With Divisive Ideology
ESEA already prohibits schools from using federal dollars provided by programs authorized under ESEA to promote sexual activity generally. Current law also prohibits ESEA funds from being used to distribute or aid in the distribution of legally obscene materials to minors on school grounds, teach sex education/ HIV prevention, or distribute contraception in schools.\5\ These prohibitions do not tell school districts how or what they can teach but merely set guardrails on how federal funds can be spent. As such, they do not infringe on the longstanding prohibition that prevents the federal government from exercising ``any direction, supervision, or control over the curriculum, program of instruction, administration, or personnel of any educational institution, school, or school system . . .''.\6\ Schools are free to use state and local funds to provide sex education and HIV prevention classes, and often do, tailoring their curricula and programs to the prevailing opinions of the locality and not the federal government.
\5\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7906. Even current law prohibitions on sex education allow for federal funds to be used if, ``that instruction is age appropriate and includes the health benefits of abstinence;''. Id.
\6\20 U.S.C. Sec. 1232a.
On its face, it would appear that the prohibition in H.R. 7661 operates in the same manner. However, the broad definitions tied to its funding restrictions could significantly affect school-based health education, library collections, curriculum, field trips, enrichment activities, and federally supported student services. The bill will likely influence local decisions about instructional materials and student support.
School districts already face pressure campaigns over books they buy for their libraries and curriculum they use in their classrooms. These campaigns often have nothing to do with the educational value or generally understood age-appropriateness of some material.\7\ For example, in Tennessee, a school board voted to remove Maus, a Pulitzer Prize-winning graphic novel, in part because of images of nudity despite its clear educational purpose as Holocaust literature.\8\ Similarly, Holocaust education materials often include documentary photographs of nude survivors or victims, not because the material is sexually provocative but because it is historical evidence of the gross inhumanity of the Holocaust.\9\ But, since H.R. 7661 deems any material that ``exposes children to nude adults''' as ``sexually explicit'' without exception, schools would have no leeway to argue that such materials, however educational or age-appropriate, were not in fact prohibited. The same issue arises with respect to materials that fulfill state curricular requirements for LGBTQ-inclusive instruction.\10\ By defining any material that ``involves gender dysphoria or transgenderism''\11\ as ``sexually oriented'', H.R. 7661 will prevent ESEA funds from being used to purchase such materials, even if they only contain age-appropriate, non-sexually explicit material.
\7\Tovia Smith, School Book Bans Show no Signs of Slowing, New PEN America Report Finds, NPR, Sep. 21, 2023, https://www.npr.org/2023/09/ 21/1200725104/book-bans-school-pen-america.
\8\Tim Stelloh, `Maus,' Pulitzer Prize-winning Book about Holocaust, is Pulled from Tennessee School District, NBC News, Jan. 27, 2022, https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/maus-pulitzer-prize-winning-book-holocaust-pulled-tennessee-school-dis-rcna13730.
\9\Group Portrait of Naked Survivors in Mauthausen Concentration Camp, U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, May 05, 1945, https:// collections.ushmm.org/search/catalog/pa1032317.
\10\Equality Maps: LGBTQ Curricular Laws, Movement Advancement Project, Apr. 20, 2026, https://www.lgbtmap.org/equality-maps/ curricular_laws.
\11\It is worth noting ``trangenderism'' is recognized as hate speech by Gay & Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation (GLAAD). Online Anti-LGBTQ Hate Terms Defined: `Transgenderism', GLAAD, https:// glaad.org/transgenderism-definition-meaning-anti-lgbt-online-hate/.
Supporters of H.R. 7661 would say that the bill is not prohibiting schools from teaching or purchasing anything--it is simply prohibiting what can be done with federal money. In this case this is a distinction without a difference. It has been established that certain curricula material like textbooks vary depending on the state they are used in.\12\ Commonly Texas and California are cited as the two large markets that drive left v. right editorial differences in textbooks.\13\ But, H.R. 7661 inserts a third player in these markets, the federal government. The bill's prohibitions would supersede state preferences since schools in any state might use funds to purchase textbooks or other curricular materials. As such, publishers that do not adhere to H.R. 7661's prohibitions could find their materials remaining unsold on the shelf. While it is not direct, H.R. 7661 would unleash an indirect censorship power over any school that receives ESEA funds. ESEA funds can support a wide array of activities including teacher salaries, programs to help students meet challenging state academic standards, well-rounded education services, and school-based mental health programs. Any service or program where a transgender student or teacher could be involved would force a school to confront whether ESEA funds could be used, or if doing so would involve ``transgenderism'' or ``gender dysphoria''. In practice this would be an unworkable standard for schools. Schools should be able to use federal dollars without the threat of micromanagement of every decision to determine if it adheres to the Majority's ideology.
\12\E.g., Dana Goldstein, Two States. Eight Textbooks. Two American Stories, N.Y. Times, Jan. 12, 2020, https://www.nytimes.com/ interactive/2020/01/12/us/texas-vs-california-history-textbooks.html.
\13\Id.
Finally, it must be noted that H.R. 7661 does include a rule of construction that prevents the bill from interfering with the teaching of ``standard science coursework'', ``the texts of major world religions'', ``classic works of literature'' or ``classic works of art.''\14\ This again puts the federal government at the center of determining what will be taught in schools since H.R. 7661 includes definitions of both classic works of literature and art. Those definitions come in part from materials published by Compass Classroom, a provider of homeschool curricula whose website prominently promotes its ``Christian worldview'' and ability to ``[t]each your kids to think Biblically about the world.''\15\ In its letter of opposition, the publisher Penguin Random House expressed the problems inherent in H.R. 7661's approach:
\14\H.R. 7661 Sec. 2, 119th Cong. (2026).
\15\Compass Classroom, Christian Homeschool Video Curriculum, https://compassclassroom.com/ (last visited June 17, 2026).
Rather than allowing educators and librarians to
select appropriate titles that reflect the maturity,
reading ability, and interests of their students, H.R.
7661 offers subjective and often biased lists of
``classics''' assembled by Encyclopedia Britannica, and
two reading lists published by a single curriculum
provider, Compass Classroom, written by Thomas Purifoy,
Jr. and Mary Pierson Purifoy. If a book is not a
classic in the eyes of those three sources, it is
deemed unworthy of consideration. Not only does this
rule out classic titles such as The Great Gatsby (F.
Scott Fitzgerald), Of Mice and Men (John Steinbeck),
and The Crucible (Arthur Miller) it also forbids
consideration of any new works.
While framed as addressing explicit content, the
bill's ambiguous language and definitions extend beyond
explicit material to include content related to
identity and ideology, narrowing the range of stories
and perspectives available to students of all
identities and backgrounds. Reading fosters empathy,
critical thinking, and civic understanding, and when
access to books is limited, these benefits are
diminished. Furthermore, being able to read,
comprehend, and interpret philosophically complex and
ambiguous writing such as Fitzgerald, Steinbeck and
Miller mentioned above is crucial to honing independent
thinking skills that are routinely called for on
standard college admission exams.\16\
\16\Letter from Skip Dye, Sr. Vice-Pres. & Dir. Sales Operations & Library Sales, Penguin Random House, to H. Comm. on Educ. & Workforce (Apr. 13, 2026), https://global. penguinrandomhouse.com/announcements/penguin-random-house-sends-letter-to-congress-urging -opposition-to-h-r-7661/.
The Bill Does Nothing To Address Genuine Issues for Schools and
Students and Intentionally Causes Harm for a Vulnerable
Population of Young People
While the Majority continues to center culture war issues as Committee business, K-12 schools continue to face pressing issues. H.R. 7661 does nothing to address the slew of concerns public schools have faced since this Administration began. Last year, the Department of Education (ED) failed to disburse over $6 billion of federally mandated funds to schools and organizations on time creating chaos and forcing schools and districts to scramble to ensure services continued for students.\17\ Additionally, a court ruled the Administration could move forward with canceling all Teacher Quality Partnership (TQP) and Supporting Effective Educator Development (SEED) grants\18\ at a time when educator preparedness is at a crisis level in many states.\19\ Finally, the Administration is attempting to illegally dismantle ED through executive order,\20\ interagency agreements (IAAs),\21\ and a Reduction in Force (RIF) which cut ED staff in half,\22\ and most recently, plans to shutter the doors of ED's headquarters.\23\ Now is simply not the time to consider H.R. 7661.
\17\Lexi Cochran, Trump Administration Withholding $6B for After- School, Summer Programs, The Hill, Jul. 02, 2025, https://thehill.com/ homenews/education/5381348-trump-administration-after-school-funding-summer-programs/.
